subject: history
title: The 1973 Oil Shock: One Cut, One Price Jump

segments.say: Before the shock: oil flows freely at about $3 a barrel. Crude oil moves steadily from the OPEC oil fields to importing countries along one supply route, and the world price sits at about $3 a barrel. Point at the open route and the price label on your student notes before the valve closes.
questions: Where does the oil flow from and to in this scene?
What is the world oil price before the shock, and what keeps it there?

segments.say: October 1973: the embargo closes the valve on the flow. OPEC embargoes oil exports to selected importing countries, no oil crosses the closed valve, and the price bar jumps from about $3 to about $12 a barrel - roughly four times higher. Now try the price-jump questions on your worksheet.
questions: What exactly does the embargo cut?
By how much does the world oil price jump, and why?

segments.say: Stage by stage: dearer oil becomes dearer everything. Dearer fuel raises transport costs first, dearer transport and energy raise factory costs next, and factories pass those costs on so shop prices rise last. Check the order of the three stages against your student notes before moving on.
questions: Which stage rises first after the oil price jump, and why?
Why do shop prices rise last in the chain?

segments.say: Spending falls back: households buy less. Prices stay high while the spending bar falls, and importing economies slow. Keep the whole chain - embargo, price jump, transport, factories, shops, falling demand - in view as you check your student notes and finish the exit ticket.
questions: What happens to household spending at the end of the chain, and why?
What is the whole oil-shock chain, in order?
segments.watchFor: The 1973 oil crisis pushed prices up because governments printed extra money to pay for dearer oil. Listen for students who start the chain with money or spending instead of the cut in supply. Send them back to scene 2 and the closed valve: The price rises started on the supply side, not the money side: the OPEC embargo cut the flow of oil, the world oil price jumped from about $3 to about $12 a barrel, and because oil and transport are inputs to almost everything, that one rise was passed on stage by stage into transport costs, factory costs and shop prices while households cut spending back.
